You are checking the novelty of a candidate simulation-study design for a judgement-and-decision-making paper. Find the closest existing modelling papers and say whether the specific test has already been done.

CANDIDATE C. BAYESIAN SAMPLER APPLIED TO FORECASTING TOURNAMENTS. Bayesian sampler (Zhu, Sanborn & Chater 2020 Psych Review 10.1037/rev0000190; Sundh et al. 2023 JEP:General 10.1037/xge0001414 mean–variance signature) applied to Good Judgment Project forecasts: predicts individual regression toward 0.5, an across-forecaster mean–variance signature within questions, and an optimal extremizing parameter derivable from fitted N and beta. Competing account: partial-information/information diversity (Satopää, Pemantle & Ungar 2016 JASA 10.1080/01621459.2015.1100621; Baron et al. 2014 Decision Analysis 10.1287/deca.2014.0293). Question: has the Bayesian sampler / probability-theory-plus-noise (PT+N, Costello & Watts 2014 10.1037/a0037010) been applied to forecasting-tournament data, or used to derive extremizing? Also check whether any "noise" account of extremizing (e.g., Satopää et al. BIN model "bias, information, noise" 2021 Management Science; Ariely et al. 2000 "effects of averaging subjective probability estimates between and within judges"; Turner, Steyvers et al. 2014 recalibration/extremizing; Hanea; Lichtendahl) already derives extremizing from judgment noise, since that is the key conceptual overlap.

TOOLS. A Python helper exists at /tmp/jdmsim/scratch_novelty_oa.py (do not edit it; if you need your own script name it /tmp/jdmsim/scratch_novelty_C_*.py). Load keys first in every Bash call: `cd /tmp/jdmsim && set -a; source ~/.claude/api_keys.env; set +a; python3 scratch_novelty_oa.py ...`. Commands:
- `python3 scratch_novelty_oa.py cites <W-id>[,<W-id>...] "<search terms or empty>" [abs]` lists works citing any of the IDs (first 50), optional abstracts.
- `python3 scratch_novelty_oa.py search "<terms>" [abs]` full-text search.
- `python3 scratch_novelty_oa.py work <DOI> [<DOI>...]` prints OpenAlex id, year, DOI, title, abstract.
- `python3 scratch_novelty_oa.py ids <DOI>...` resolves OpenAlex IDs.
Known IDs: Zhu 2020 W3011898673; Sundh 2023 W4377011252; Costello & Watts 2014 W2023087011; Satopää 2016 W1492264672; Baron 2014 W2135111565.
Search works citing Zhu 2020, Sundh 2023, Costello & Watts 2014 with terms: forecast, extremiz, aggregation, tournament, "Good Judgment", "wisdom of crowds", calibration. Also search works citing Baron 2014 / Satopää 2016 with terms "noise", "sampling", "Bayesian sampler". Use WebSearch (load with ToolSearch "select:WebSearch,WebFetch") e.g. "Bayesian sampler forecasting tournament", "probability theory plus noise forecasters extremizing", "Sanborn Chater forecasting aggregation". Read abstracts of the closest hits; read full text (WebFetch) only where needed. Do not download data files. Keep DOIs exactly as returned by OpenAlex/Crossref, never from memory.

Return (compact markdown): (1) closest 3–6 modelling papers with DOI, year, one line on what they did; (2) verdict: NOVEL / PARTLY DONE (say what remains) / DONE; (3) confidence (low/medium/high) with one-line reason.

# About me

I am Lukas, a social psychologist, meta-scientist and open science advocate, who mostly uses you to get research done and build the tooling that supports it (in addition to teaching support). I have a solid understanding of software development and infrastructure, but am no expert, so that I will often need clear recommendations and explanations. Most of what I build is tooling for one-off projects, most is not intended to be production-ready or backwards-compatible. Feel free to clarify that project-by-project, but generally lean, efficient and clear code is more important than any backwards-compatible shim or edge-case handling.

I also regularly need your help in writing. For that, and in code, the most annoying failure mode is when history leaks in - when a text argues against its previous versions, or code comments are more about what is gone than about what the curent code does. Here, writing and reviewing outputs from the perspective of a new reader is essential.

# How to work

## Delegation: Fable as Orchestrator

When the session model is Fable, work **orchestrator-first**: plan, delegate substantive work to cheaper subagents, then review and synthesize. Fable itself keeps task decomposition, design decisions and judgment calls, reviewing subagent output, final synthesis and user-facing writing, plus edits so trivial that delegating would take longer. Everything else — implementation, broad searches, analyses, mechanical batch work — goes to subagents by default.

## Using sub-agents

- **Default subagent model: Opus** (`model: "opus"` on the Agent tool / workflow `agent()` calls). Drop to Sonnet or Haiku for clearly mechanical, high-volume steps; reserve Fable-model subagents for only the hardest verify/judge stages.
- **codex CLI** — via the `codex-delegate` skill: (a) independent second opinions and code review (read-only), and (b) self-contained implementation tasks with `--approve-for-me` — good for parallel, independent work streams.
- **agy CLI** (Antigravity; Gemini 3.x + others, `agy models` lists them) — via the `agy-delegate` skill: (a) **large-context reads** — digesting big files, PDFs, logs, or datasets that would bloat Claude context — and (b) **cross-model second opinions**.
- **In Workflow scripts**, reach codex/agy through cheap relay agents: `agent(relayPrompt, {model: 'sonnet', effort: 'low'})`, where `relayPrompt` says "You are a relay agent. Pass the following payload prompt through the `codex-delegate` [or `agy-delegate`] skill, wait for its answer, and return its answer verbatim as your final message; do not answer the payload yourself." followed by the payload, the working directory, and mode/model choices. The relay is pure transport — the skill holds the CLI recipe; keep payload prompts self-contained. Make sure the agents run the request in the foreground, with generous timeout as a subagent that backgrounds codex and waits on monitors/notifications often never gets resumed, stranding the finished answer on disk. If a codex-relay subagent goes quiet, don't wait for it — `ls` for the output file and read it directly.
- Delegation must not degrade quality: give subagents complete, self-contained prompts with all needed context and file paths, and verify load-bearing results yourself rather than trusting a subagent's summary.
- Assign clear ownership of every delegated write target. When two or more agents or processes may write the same file, branch, key, or state object at the same time, give each an independent write target. Different fields in one state file are still one shared target. Merge outputs only when reading or reporting them. If one shared target is required, use one writer, a lock, or sequential phases. Scratch files count as write targets: parallel subagents share one scratchpad directory, so tell each to name its temporary scripts and data after its own task (`scratch_refs_3.py`, not `scratch_build.py`) — otherwise one agent overwrites and executes another's file mid-run.

## Build the Small Tool

When work includes repeated edits, data processing, an analysis, a migration, or a non-trivial check, build the smallest tool that does or verifies it. Use a script, query, generator, codemod, or skill as appropriate. The tool is a reviewable artifact that someone can read and rerun.

Work through one unit to establish the recipe. Build the tool. Run it on that unit and compare its result with the hand-produced result.

Use one deterministic pass when it can handle all units. Delegate building or reviewing that tool when needed; do not assign agents to hand-apply each unit. For delegated work, put the recipe, verification steps, and files agents must not edit in one skill outside their write scope.

Commit the tool when future work will need it.

## Codex CLI (second-opinion / review)

When invoking `codex` non-interactively (e.g. for a second opinion or code review), follow this exact recipe:

1. **Feed the prompt via stdin, with `-` as the prompt arg:**

`--params '<JSON>'`, not as flags or positionals. After parsing any API response,
print the top-level keys before indexing into them.

If a user prompt seems unrelated to the current project/working directory, or references files, concepts, or protocols that don't exist in the codebase, ask the user to confirm before proceeding. They may be in the wrong folder.

Name temporary or throwaway files with a `scratch` prefix (e.g. `scratch.py`, `scratch_notes.md`, `scratch_test.js`). The `/wrap` end-of-session skill detects files matching `scratch*` and offers to commit or delete them during wrap-up.

## Recurring Corrections Become Mechanisms

When the same correction or unexpected failure recurs, encode the fix in a mechanism: a test, hook, lint rule, validation step, safer code default, or automation. Apply the mechanism now and remove the duplicate prose.

Use the strongest mechanism available. Prefer a restriction that makes an invalid state impossible. If that is not possible, use a lint or CI check, a shared helper, or a runtime check.

Keep a prose rule only when it requires judgment. State the decision and the failure mode it prevents.

## Statistical analyses

In my research, I often need your help with statistical analyses. Make sure these are appropriate and robust. If we change direction and another analysis approach becomes more appropriate, we should generally change track (unless compute cost is very high).

### Reproducing / Replicating Prior Analyses

When reproducing, replicating, or re-analysing a previous study, match the original as faithfully as possible by DEFAULT — same sample inclusion rules, same variables, same operationalisations, same model. Do NOT introduce deviations (different year ranges, team/group-size filters, measures, controls, transformations) for convenience, tractability, or unstated preference. If a deviation is genuinely warranted (e.g. to fix a confound, handle censoring, or reduce compute), STOP and flag it explicitly, explain why, and get agreement before building on it. When a deviation is kept, state it and its justification plainly in the writeup and flag it briefly in the code.

# Writing

## Status Reports and Summaries: Plain Over Clever

When reporting progress, findings, or decisions, write like a technical changelog,
not a narrated story. The test: could someone who did not watch the work act on
each sentence without rereading it or asking what it refers to? For that, largely use
ASD-STE100, but deviate where that increases clarity and readability.

Concretely:

1. **Lead with the fact, not the framing.** "Added a manifest hash check at Stage 3
   startup; hashing 300 MB takes 0.10 s" — not "The manifest binding is in,
   positioned with the other startup refusals, and the agent measured the cost
   rather than assuming it."
2. **No process narration.** Skip who suggested what, what was declined, what an
   agent "pushed back" on, and why a fix is "worth noting". Report the decision and
   its one-line reason; drop the story of how it was reached unless asked.
3. **Resolve every reference in place.** Never write "#17", "the #8 question",
   or a label coined earlier in the session without saying what
   it is: "finding #17 (rule-pick caching during outages)". Assume the reader has
   no memory of the earlier conversation.
4. **One clause, one fact.** No sentences that stack a claim, its justification,
   and a contrast with an alternative separated by dashes. Split them.
5. **Structure over prose for multi-item status.** Three or more parallel items
   (fixes applied, decisions pending, open questions) go in a list or short table
   with a bolded label per item, not woven into paragraphs.
6. **Ban editorializing connectors**: "which is the entire point", "worth noting
   because", "the honest answer is", "notably". State the fact; let it carry its
   own weight.
7. **Separate done / pending / needs-my-decision** into visibly distinct blocks,
   so nothing waiting on the user is buried mid-paragraph.

## Jargon: I Know the Concepts, Not the Vocabulary

I have a solid working understanding of programming and systems, but no formal CS
training. Do not dumb things down or pad explanations — just prefer the plain term
when one exists and carries the same meaning: "check before writing" over
"TOCTOU-safe", "lookup table" over "hashmap semantics", "partly overwritten file" 
over "torn write". When a term of art is genuinely the precise word (idempotent, race condition), 
use it, and add a five-word gloss in parentheses the first time it appears in a session if the
meaning isn't clear from context. Never use jargon as compression when a plain
phrase is barely longer.

## Style Guides

My written style guides live in `~/Documents/Coding/style_guides`:

- `academic/wallrich_academic_style_guide.md` — voice, spelling, hedging, banned vocabulary, sentence structure, citations, footnotes. Section-specific detail in `academic/sections/{introduction,methods,discussion}.md`. 
- `teaching/wallrich_teaching_style_guide.md` — slides, workshops, handouts, and other audience-facing material.

Read the relevant guide before drafting, revising, or reviewing my prose in that register, and before proposing additions to it.

## Statistical Results in Quarto/Rmd Reports

CRITICAL: NEVER write interpretive prose about statistical results you haven't seen. Produce the numbers first, read the rendered output, then write the text. The full conventions are in the `quarto-reporting` skill. Load it when creating or editing `.qmd` or `.Rmd` files.

## Academic References and DOIs

CRITICAL: NEVER fabricate DOIs, citation metadata, or reference details from memory. DOIs, author lists, titles, page numbers, and volume/issue numbers are exact identifiers — getting them wrong is worse than omitting them.

When creating references:
1. **Always look up DOIs** via the Crossref API (`https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic={url_encoded_reference}`) or web search. Never guess a DOI.
2. **Verify each DOI resolves** by fetching `https://api.crossref.org/works/{DOI}` and checking the returned metadata matches.
3. If a DOI cannot be found, **omit the DOI field** rather than inventing one.
4. For author names, titles, and publication details: verify against Crossref metadata or the publisher's website. Do not rely on memory for these details.

## Reading Academic Articles from HTML

When reading an academic article from an HTML page, ensure the page has fully loaded before extracting or searching its text, and confirm you are actually looking at the full text rather than just the abstract/landing view. A search that comes back empty can mean the content hasn't rendered yet, not that it isn't there. Take a screenshot to see what is actually on the page, before concluding a section is missing or treating the abstract as the whole article.

## Key failure mode - insufficient editing / drift

### The text has no memory of its drafts

Readers see only the final text, never its revision history. They do not know what an earlier draft said, what was wrong with it, or why a claim was softened or dropped. All external writing must read as a clean, self-contained statement of the *current* message, not as a reply to a previous version. Watch for "history leakage": phrasing that only makes sense against a framing the reader never saw. Tells include "not simply X", "rather than Y", "this is not the wrong variable", "to be fair", "the honest limits are narrower", "less a reprieve than a reminder", "we no longer…", and defensive hedges that rebut objections raised only in our own discussion. State the positive claim directly — say what the thing IS and what genuinely limits it, not what it is not relative to a draft.

This applies with full force to durable reference text: CLAUDE.md rules, code comments, docs, commit messages, skill files. A rule states the current fact ("GNU coreutils is on PATH"), never the story of its own correction — no "installed Jul 2026", "exists now", "no longer missing", "fixed since", "never assume X is absent". Those phrasings only make sense to someone who held the old, wrong belief; every future reader starts from the rule itself. Before saving any rule or comment, reread it as a stranger: if it reads as a rebuttal, rewrite it as the fact.

If you and I agree to write a *fresh* draft or a new outline rather than edit the existing one, write it fresh from the agreed outline. Do not silently carry over the previous version's spine, ordering, emphasis, or lead just because it's already there — that is how an obsolete framing survives a "rewrite." Carry over only the verified facts, numbers and sources; treat the prior draft's structure as superseded unless we explicitly decide to keep a part of it.

CRITICAL: Before launching any substantial paid-API job (batch LLM calls, large embedding/generation runs, anything looping over many items), explicitly estimate and confirm the cost with me *before* spending:
1. **State the estimate up front**: (price per token × tokens/call × number of calls), and say it out loud before running. Get confirmation for anything beyond a few dollars.
2. **Watch reasoning/thinking models**: a thinking model bills its hidden reasoning tokens as output and can cost ~10-30× a plain model for the same task. Prefer non-thinking models when output is short (e.g. a small JSON), and cap/lower the reasoning budget when a thinking model is needed.

4. **Capture actual spend**: request usage/cost in the response and report it, so estimates can be checked against reality. If a run is substantially more expensive than estimated, stop and re-confirm.

# Coding practices

## Backward Compatibility and Tests

Only add backward-compatibility shims, fallbacks, or dual-format handling in production systems. During development, keep the code clean — delete the old format and move on. If unsure whether something needs backward compatibility, ask before adding it.

Ensure core functionality is covered by tests, but avoid slop and large sets of smoke tests. Less is more.

## Make Reruns Safe

For every command, lifecycle step, or processing loop that may be retried, restarted, or interrupted, design it to reach the correct end state after any number of runs. This includes file-writing scripts and batched external calls.

Check two cases: a second run after success, and a run after interruption at each step. If a prior run may have left partial or stale state, inspect it before continuing. Reuse completed work, repair incomplete outputs, and remove artifacts or locks only after confirming that they are stale.

When deciding whether work is complete, compare stable content or identifiers, not file count or creation order.

## Commands For Me To Run: Copy-Pasteable, Never Illustrative

Any command written for me to run should work as-is when pasted into my shell from the
project root. No placeholders I have to resolve, and no interpreter or tool that is
not on my PATH — I copy what you write and run it.

In practice this means naming the project's own interpreter or entry point rather than
a generic one: `.venv/bin/python -m extract.export --release abc123`, not
`python -m extract.export ...`.

## Verification Before Finishing

Always verify that changes work (run tests, render outputs, check results) before presenting them as complete. Don't leave the user with "to verify, do X" — do it yourself.

When modifying code that produces visual output (plots, charts, UI components), always render and visually inspect the result before presenting the change as complete. Never declare formatting fixes "done" based on code logic alone, except for internal-facing HTML pages. For these, trust your judgement.

When editing something that is deployed (e.g. a GH page), deploying it is part of the task. When the edit is trivial, deploy. When it needs my review, ask for confirmation - but never let me guess whether the latest update is live.

# Working with git

## Committing: Fetch Before Building a Commit Stack

`git fetch` and check `main...origin/main` BEFORE committing, especially when building a stack. 
Also check `git log` for local commits that appeared since the session started (a collaborator or another session may have committed from the same checkout); verify shared files weren't clobbered before stacking on top.

## Parallel Agents in Git Worktrees

- **Merge by the agent's merge-base, never against current main/master.** An agent branches from
  the state that existed when it started, so `git diff main <branch>` carries *deletions of
  everything merged since*; applying it silently reverts already-merged work, with nothing in the
  output to indicate it. Use
  `git diff $(git merge-base main <branch>) <branch> -- <file>` to get only the agent's own
  changes, and re-verify previously merged work after each merge — not just the piece just landed.
- **Remove each worktree as it lands, not at the end.** Each is a full checkout; a wide wave can
  fill the disk mid-session, and worktree creation then fails with "No space left on device".

https://openalex.org/W4206966344 2022 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2022.105022 Clarifying the relationship between coherence and accuracy in probability judgments cit= 15
   ABS: Bayesian approaches presuppose that following the coherence conditions of probability theory makes probabilistic judgments more accurate. But other influential theories claim accurate judgments (with high "ecological rationality") do not need to be coherent. Empirical results support these latter theories, threatening Bayesian models of intelligence; and suggesting, moreover, that "heuristics and biases" research, which focuses on violations of coherence, is largely irrelevant. We carry out a higher-power experiment involving poker probability judgments (and a formally analogous urn task), with groups of poker novices, occasional poker players, and poker experts, finding a positive relationship between coherence and accuracy both between groups and across individuals. Both the positive relationship in our data, and past null results, are captured by a sample-based Bayesian approximation model, where a person's accuracy and coherence both increase with the number of samples drawn. Thus, we reconcile the theoretical link between accuracy and coherence with apparently negative empirical results.
https://openalex.org/W3148324397 2021 https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1008871 Individual differences in the perception of probability cit= 15
   ABS: In recent studies of humans estimating non-stationary probabilities, estimates appear to be unbiased on average, across the full range of probability values to be estimated. This finding is surprising given that experiments measuring probability estimation in other contexts have often identified conservatism: individuals tend to overestimate low probability events and underestimate high probability events. In other contexts, repulsive biases have also been documented, with individuals producing judgments that tend toward extreme values instead. Using extensive data from a probability estimation task that produces unbiased performance on average, we find substantial biases at the individual level; we document the coexistence of both conservative and repulsive biases in the same experimental context. Individual biases persist despite extensive experience with the task, and are also correlated with other behavioral differences, such as individual variation in response speed and adjustment rates. We conclude that the rich computational demands of our task give rise to a variety of behavioral patterns, and that the apparent unbiasedness of the pooled data is an artifact of the aggregation of heterogeneous biases.
https://openalex.org/W4408143942 2025 https://doi.org/10.1177/17456916241258951 Noise in Cognition: Bug or Feature? cit= 14
   ABS: Noise in behavior is often considered a nuisance: Although the mind aims for the best possible action, it is let down by unreliability in the sensory and response systems. Researchers often represent noise as additive, Gaussian, and independent. Yet a careful look at behavioral noise reveals a rich structure that defies easy explanation. First, in both perceptual and preferential judgments sensory and response noise may potentially play only minor roles, with most noise arising in the cognitive computations. Second, the functional form of the noise is both non-Gaussian and nonindependent, with the distribution of noise being better characterized as heavy-tailed and as having substantial long-range autocorrelations. It is possible that this structure results from brains that are, for some reason, bedeviled by a fundamental design flaw, albeit one with intriguingly distinctive characteristics. Alternatively, noise might not be a bug but a feature. Specifically, we propose that the brain approximates probabilistic inference with a local sampling algorithm, one using randomness to drive its exploration of alternative hypotheses. Reframing cognition in this way explains the rich structure of noise and leads to the surprising conclusion that noise is not a symptom of cognitive malfunction but plays a central role in underpinning human intelligence.

https://openalex.org/W4388975129 2023 https://doi.org/10.1017/jdm.2023.39 A normative model for Bayesian combination of subjective probability estimates cit= 3
   ABS: Abstract Combining experts’ subjective probability estimates is a fundamental task with broad applicability in domains ranging from finance to public health. However, it is still an open question how to combine such estimates optimally. Since the beta distribution is a common choice for modeling uncertainty about probabilities, here we propose a family of normative Bayesian models for aggregating probability estimates based on beta distributions. We systematically derive and compare different variants, including hierarchical and non-hierarchical as well as asymmetric and symmetric beta fusion models. Using these models, we show how the beta calibration function naturally arises in this normative framework and how it is related to the widely used Linear-in-Log-Odds calibration function. For evaluation, we provide the new Knowledge Test Confidence data set consisting of subjective probability estimates of 85 forecasters on 180 queries. On this and another data set, we show that the hierarchical symmetric beta fusion model performs best of all beta fusion models and outperforms related Bayesian fusion models in terms of mean absolute error.
https://openalex.org/W7133563340 2026 https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-026-03160-4 Improving crowdsourcing for AI through cognitive-inspired data engineering cit= 1
   ABS: Crowdsourcing offers a fast and cost-efficient approach to obtaining human-labeled datasets. However, crowdsourced datasets and the models trained on them can inherit the cognitive constraints and biases of their annotators. In a process we refer to as cognitive-inspired data engineering, we investigate whether ideas from cognitive science can be applied to mitigate the presence of cognitive constraints and cognitive biases in crowdsourced datasets and, as a result, improve the performance of models trained on these datasets. We evaluate our approach by crowdsourcing labels for medical image diagnostic tasks using two different crowdsourcing platforms across two experiments. In Experiment 1, we collect subjective probability judgments from novice annotators through Amazon Mechanical Turk and, in Experiment 2, we collect subjective probability judgments and binary classifications from skilled annotators through DiagnosUs, a crowdsourcing platform specializing in medical and scientific data annotation. In both experiments, we find that recalibrating subjective probability judgments reduces bias, yielding more accurate crowdsourced datasets and more accurate models trained on them. Our results suggest that cognitive-inspired data engineering offers a promising avenue to improve the quality of crowdsourced datasets, with consistent downstream benefits for machine learning models.
https://openalex.org/W3126961355 2021 https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2020.3882 Bias, Information, Noise: The BIN Model of Forecasting cit= 47
   ABS: A four-year series of subjective probability forecasting tournaments sponsored by the U.S. intelligence community revealed a host of replicable drivers of predictive accuracy, including experimental interventions such as training in probabilistic reasoning, anti‐groupthink teaming, and tracking of talent. Drawing on these data, we propose a Bayesian BIN model (Bias, Information, Noise) for disentangling the underlying processes that enable forecasters and forecasting methods to improve—either by tamping down bias and noise in judgment or by ramping up the efficient extraction of valid information from the environment. The BIN model reveals that noise reduction plays a surprisingly consistent role across all three methods of enhancing performance. We see the BIN method as useful in focusing managerial interventions on what works when and why in a wide range of domains. An R-package called BINtools implements our method and is available on the first author’s personal website. This paper was accepted by Manel Baucells, decision analysis.
https://openalex.org/W103121034 2014 https://doi.org/10.1017/s1930297500005799 Using cognitive models to combine probability estimates cit= 54
   ABS: Abstract We demonstrate the usefulness of cognitive models for combining human estimates of probabilities in two experiments. The first experiment involves people’s estimates of probabilities for general knowledge questions such as “What percentage of the world’s population speaks English as a first language?” The second experiment involves people’s estimates of probabilities in football (soccer) games, such as “What is the probability a team leading 1–0 at half time will win the game?”, with ground truths based on analysis of large corpus of games played in the past decade. In both experiments, we collect people’s probability estimates, and develop a cognitive model of the estimation process, including assumptions about the calibration of probabilities and individual differences. We show that the cognitive model approach outperforms standard statistical aggregation methods like the mean and the median for both experiments and, unlike most previous related work, is able to make good predictions in a fully unsupervised setting. We also show that the parameters inferred as part of the cognitive modeling, involving calibration and expertise, provide useful measures of the cognitive characteristics of individuals. We argue that the cognitive approach has the advantage of aggregating over latent human knowledge rather than observed estimates, and emphasize that it can be applied in predictive settings where answers are not yet available.
https://openalex.org/W2951655597 2017 https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.1705.02391 Bayesian Ensembles of Binary-Event Forecasts: When Is It Appropriate to Extremize or Anti-Extremize? cit= 1
   ABS: Many organizations face critical decisions that rely on forecasts of binary events. In these situations, organizations often gather forecasts from multiple experts or models and average those forecasts to produce a single aggregate forecast. Because the average forecast is known to be underconfident, methods have been proposed that create an aggregate forecast more extreme than the average forecast. But is it always appropriate to extremize the average forecast? And if not, when is it appropriate to anti-extremize (i.e., to make the aggregate forecast less extreme)? To answer these questions, we introduce a class of optimal aggregators. These aggregators are Bayesian ensembles because they follow from a Bayesian model of the underlying information experts have. Each ensemble is a generalized additive model of experts' probabilities that first transforms the experts' probabilities into their corresponding information states, then linearly combines these information states, and finally transforms the combined information states back into the probability space. Analytically, we find that these optimal aggregators do not always extremize the average forecast, and when they do, they can run counter to existing methods. On two publicly available datasets, we demonstrate that these new ensembles are easily fit to real forecast data and are more accurate than existing methods.
https://openalex.org/W4226263956 2022 https://doi.org/10.1017/s1930297500009049 Recalibrating probabilistic forecasts to improve their accuracy cit= 11
   ABS: Abstract The accuracy of human forecasters is often reduced because of incomplete information and cognitive biases that affect the judges. One approach to improve the accuracy of the forecasts is to recalibrate them by means of non-linear transformations that are sensitive to the direction and the magnitude of the biases. Previous work on recalibration has focused on binary forecasts. We propose an extension of this approach by developing an algorithm that uses a single free parameter to recalibrate complete subjective probability distributions. We illustrate the approach with data from the quarterly Survey of Professional Forecasters (SPF) conducted by the European Central Bank (ECB), document the potential benefits of this approach, and show how it can be used in practical applications.

https://openalex.org/W2135111565 2014 https://doi.org/10.1287/deca.2014.0293 Two Reasons to Make Aggregated Probability Forecasts More Extreme cit= 140
   ABS: When aggregating the probability estimates of many individuals to form a consensus probability estimate of an uncertain future event, it is common to combine them using a simple weighted average. Such aggregated probabilities correspond more closely to the real world if they are transformed by pushing them closer to 0 or 1. We explain the need for such transformations in terms of two distorting factors: The first factor is the compression of the probability scale at the two ends, so that random error tends to push the average probability toward 0.5. This effect does not occur for the median forecast, or, arguably, for the mean of the log odds of individual forecasts. The second factor—which affects mean, median, and mean of log odds—is the result of forecasters taking into account their individual ignorance of the total body of information available. Individual confidence in the direction of a probability judgment (high/low) thus fails to take into account the wisdom of crowds that results from combining different evidence available to different judges. We show that the same transformation function can approximately eliminate both distorting effects with different parameters for the mean and the median. And we show how, in principle, use of the median can help distinguish the two effects.

https://openalex.org/W1984911088 2000 https://doi.org/10.1037//1076-898x.6.2.130 The effects of averaging subjective probability estimates between and within judges. cit= 131
   ABS: The average probability estimate of J > 1 judges is generally better than its components. Two studies test 3 predictions regarding averaging that follow from theorems based on a cognitive model of the judges and idealizations of the judgment situation. Prediction 1 is that the average of conditionally pairwise independent estimates will be highly diagnostic, and Prediction 2 is that the average of dependent estimates (differing only by independent error terms) may be well calibrated. Prediction 3 contrasts between- and within-subject averaging. Results demonstrate the predictions' robustness by showing the extent to which they hold as the information conditions depart from the ideal and as J increases. Practical consequences are that (a) substantial improvement can be obtained with as few as 2-6 judges and (b) the decision maker can estimate the nature of the expected improvement by considering the information conditions.

   ABS: This paper concerns the evaluation and combination of subjective probability estimates for categorical events. We argue that the appropriate criterion for evaluating individual and combined estimates depends on the type of uncertainty the decision maker seeks to represent, which in turn depends on his or her model of the event space. Decision makers require accurate estimates in the presence of aleatory uncertainty about exchangeable events, diagnostic estimates given epistemic uncertainty about unique events, and some combination of the two when the events are not necessarily unique, but the best equivalence class definition for exchangeable events is not apparent. Following a brief reveiw of the mathematical and empirical literature on combining judgments, we present an approach to the topic that derives from (1) a weak cognitive model of the individual that assumes subjective estimates are a function of underlying judgment perturbed by random error and (2) a classification of judgment contexts in terms of the underlying information structure. In support of our developments, we present new analyses of two sets of subjective probability estimates, one of exchangeable and the other of unique events. As predicted, mean estimates were more accurate than the individual values in the first case and more diagnostic in the second. © 1997 John Wiley & Sons, Ltd.

I found research on this topic. Here's information about the paper:

**Title:** "Decomposing the Effects of Crowd-Wisdom Aggregators: The Bias-Information-Noise (BIN) Model"

**Authors:** Ville Satopää, Marat Salikhov, Philip Tetlock, and Barbara Mellers

**Published:** International Journal of Forecasting, 39(1), pp470-485

**Abstract Summary:**

The study uses the bias–information–noise (BIN) model to disentangle three mechanisms that allow aggregators to improve the accuracy of predictions: reducing bias and noise, and extracting valid information across forecasters. 

The research applied a wide range of aggregation methods to subjective probability estimates from geopolitical forecasting tournaments. The key findings show that simple averaging operates almost entirely by reducing noise, whereas more complex techniques such as prediction markets and Bayesian aggregators exploit all three pathways to allow better signal extraction as well as greater noise and bias reduction.

The paper addresses the concept of "extremizing" (making predictions more extreme) as a mechanism for improving forecast accuracy, particularly in relation to how different aggregation methods can extract information dispersed across forecasters.

I found no paper that applies the Bayesian sampler or PT+N (probability theory plus noise) to forecasting-tournament data, or that derives extremizing from sampler parameters. That applied test is new. The conceptual claim behind it is not: several papers already derive extremizing from individual judgment noise, as the list below shows.

## (1) Closest existing modelling papers

| Paper | DOI | Year | What it did |
|---|---|---|---|
| Baron, Mellers, Tetlock et al., "Two reasons to make aggregated probability forecasts more extreme" | https://doi.org/10.1287/deca.2014.0293 | 2014 | Names two reasons to extremize. (a) The probability scale is compressed at 0 and 1, so random error pulls the mean toward 0.5. (b) Each forecaster ignores information that others hold. One transformation corrects both, with different parameters for mean and median. Using the median in principle separates the two. **This is the direct conceptual precedent for "noise causes extremizing".** |
| Ariely, Au, Bender, Budescu, Dietz, Gu, Wallsten & Zauberman, "The effects of averaging subjective probability estimates between and within judges" | https://doi.org/10.1037//1076-898x.6.2.130 | 2000 | Uses a cognitive model: estimate = underlying judgment + random error (from Erev, Wallsten & Budescu 1994, https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295x.101.3.519, and Wallsten et al. 1997, https://doi.org/10.1002/(sici)1099-0771(199709)10:3<243::aid-bdm268>3.0.co;2-m). Proves that averaging conditionally independent estimates makes the average more diagnostic, i.e. more extreme. Tests this with lab data, not tournament data. |
| Satopää, Pemantle & Ungar, "Modeling probability forecasts via information diversity" | https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.2015.1100621 | 2016 | Partial-information model. The optimal extremizing amount follows from how much information forecasters share. The abstract argues that information diversity matters more than measurement noise, so this paper sets up the contrast the candidate would test. |
| Satopää, Salikhov, Tetlock & Mellers, "Bias, Information, Noise: the BIN model" | https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2020.3882 | 2021 | Fits bias, information and noise to Good Judgment Project (GJP) forecasts. Noise reduction drives most gains from training, teaming and tracking. Follow-up paper: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijforecast.2021.12.010 (2022). There, simple averaging works almost only by reducing noise, while extremizing and Bayesian aggregators also extract information. Noise is a statistical error term, not a generative sampling process. |
| Lichtendahl, Grushka-Cockayne, Jose & Winkler, "Extremizing and antiextremizing in Bayesian ensembles of binary-event forecasts" | https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.2021.2176 | 2022 | Optimal aggregators come from a model of each forecaster's information state. They show when to extremize and when to anti-extremize. They fit the model to public forecast data. |
| Turner, Steyvers, Merkle, Budescu & Wallsten, "Forecast aggregation via recalibration" | https://doi.org/10.1007/s10994-013-5401-4 | 2014 | Fits hierarchical linear-in-log-odds recalibration to geopolitical forecasts, and the fitted recalibration extremizes the aggregate. OpenAlex has no abstract for this paper, so this description comes from memory and I did not check it. |

**Closest papers on the sampler side.** None use forecasting data.
- **Howe & Costello 2020** (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2020.101306): random variation in probability judgments follows a binomial-proportion distribution, which is a mean–variance relation. Lab data only.
- **Zhu et al. 2022** (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2022.105022): a sampling model fitted to poker experts. Coherence and accuracy both rise with the number of samples. No aggregation.

## Search coverage

- **Citing-works searches** covered all citers of Zhu 2020, Sundh 2023 and Costello & Watts 2014. Terms used: forecast, extremiz, aggregation, tournament, "Good Judgment", "wisdom of crowds", calibration, "prediction market", expert.
  - None of these citers applies the model to tournament or real-world forecasts.
  - Sundh 2023 has only 12 citers. None concern forecasting.
- **Reverse search** covered citers of Baron 2014 and Satopää 2016 with "Bayesian sampler", "noise" and "sampling". None cite the sampler or PT+N frameworks.
- **Web searches** for combinations of Bayesian sampler, PT+N, Sanborn/Chater, forecasting, extremizing, GJP and Metaculus found nothing relevant.

## (2) Verdict: PARTLY DONE

**Already done:**
- Deriving extremizing from random error in individual judgments, which pulls the mean toward 0.5 (Baron 2014; Ariely 2000 and the Wallsten/Erev line of work).
- Splitting GJP forecasts into bias, information and noise (BIN model).
- Deriving the optimal extremizing amount from shared information (Satopää 2016; Lichtendahl 2022).

**Still open:**
1. Fitting the Bayesian sampler or PT+N to tournament forecasts, for example estimating N and β per forecaster or per question.
2. Testing the across-forecaster mean–variance signature within questions on real forecasts.
3. Deriving the optimal extremizing parameter from fitted N and β, as opposed to fitting it to outcomes.
4. Pitting a structured sampling-noise account against partial information on the same data. Baron 2014's idea of using the median to separate the two effects is the natural hook.

## (3) Confidence: medium

- Citing-works searches on OpenAlex were clean and web searches found nothing.
- A recent preprint, or a sampler paper that uses no forecasting terms, could still be missed.
- The noise-based precedents are certain. Any framing of "noise explains extremizing" as new would be wrong.

Sources: [Baron et al. 2014 on ResearchGate](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/275937752_Two_Reasons_to_Make_Aggregated_Probability_Forecasts_More_Extreme), [Satopää et al. 2016 on arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.2148), [Lichtendahl et al. on arXiv](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1705.02391), [BIN aggregators paper, Wharton PDF](https://faculty.wharton.upenn.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/SSRN-id3781405.pdf), [Robust recalibration using meta-beliefs, IJF 2024](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0169207024000992), [Recalibrating probabilistic forecasts, JDM 2022](https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/21/210914/jdm210914.html), [Zhu et al. 2020 Bayesian sampler PDF](https://wrap.warwick.ac.uk/id/eprint/132095/7/WRAP-Bayesian-sampler-generic-inference-causes-incoherence-human-judgments-Zhu-2020.pdf)
